title: Ines and the Harvest
premise: Wendell Halloran takes a teaching post in the fog-bound town of Hollowmere, where a third of each year's class vanishes before harvest and no one will say why. The town's founding families sustain themselves by feeding children to something that lives in the mirrors — an entity called the Gleaner — in exchange for another year of plenty. When Wendell's own reflection begins lagging behind reality, he discovers he is being groomed as this year's offering, and that the missing students are not dead but trapped inside the glass. With help from Ines Varga, a former student who escaped the harvest nine years ago, Wendell learns the harvest song's forbidden last verse: sung correctly, it frees the taken; sung wrong, it binds the singer forever. In the end Wendell enters the mirror to lead the trapped children out, trading his place among the living for theirs — though Ines finds a way to leave one door of the glass unlatched.
about_author: Zephyrine Brightwater is the pen name of a former rural schoolteacher who spent eleven years in farming towns where old agreements were never written down. She writes horror about institutions that keep their promises at other people's expense.

chapters.title: The Counted Doors
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. Arriving in Hollowmere, Wendell notices the school has nineteen desks but the register lists twenty-six students. The caretaker, Mrs. Aldous, shows him a ritual: count the doors at dusk, lock nothing else. Emotional beat: uneasy charm masking dread.

chapters.title: Nineteen Faces
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. First week of classes; the students are polite, hollow-eyed, and flinch when he writes on the board near the window. A girl named Petra whispers that the seventh graders 'go quiet' in October. Beat: creeping wrongness beneath normalcy.

chapters.title: Ines Varga, Absent Nine Years
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. He meets Ines, who runs the feed store and refuses to enter the school building. She warns him: when the mirrors start lagging, stop looking. He laughs it off. Beat: first ally, first dismissal.

chapters.title: One Second Behind
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. At home, his bathroom mirror reflects him raising his hand a beat after he does. By nightfall every reflective surface is delayed. He counts the doors; there is one more than yesterday. Beat: the horror becomes intimate.

chapters.title: What the Children Know
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. His students recognize the lag instantly and teach him rules without explaining them: never sing along in assembly, never answer your reflection, never be last out of the room. Beat: children as reluctant experts, tenderness and terror mixed.

chapters.title: The Harvest Song
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. Assembly practice reveals the song the whole town sings each October — three verses, everyone knows them, no one knows why the fourth line of the third verse is always mumbled. Beat: communal complicity revealed through music.

chapters.title: Petra's Drawing
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. Petra leaves a crayon drawing on his desk: figures inside a window, waving, labeled with names from old registers. One face is hers — dated next year. Beat: grief and foreknowledge; Wendell can no longer pretend.

chapters.title: Aldous Explains Nothing
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. He confronts Mrs. Aldous, who admits only that Hollowmere 'keeps its accounts current' and that the Gleaner takes what the ledger owes. She gives him salt and a small brass bell. Beat: the banality of institutional evil.

chapters.title: Ines Breaks Her Silence
chapters.summary: POV Ines. Nine years ago she was chosen, and her older brother sang the mumbled verse aloud to pull her back — it worked, and it took him instead. She tells Wendell the last verse exists, complete, in her brother's notebook. Beat: guilt, love against duty established.

chapters.title: The Notebook
chapters.summary: POV Ines. In her brother's locked room they find the transcription, water-damaged, the final lines legible only under lamplight held at an angle. Reading them aloud makes the house lights dim in rhythm. Beat: hope with a price tag.

chapters.title: Rehearsal
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. They practice singing the verse alone in the feed store; each attempt pulls their reflections slightly further out of sync. Ines realizes the song must be sung from inside the glass to work fully. Beat: dawning cost of the plan.

chapters.title: The Ledger Room
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. Beneath the school, Wendell finds a room of ledgers recording two centuries of names, including his own, entered the day he was hired. His signature is already there, in handwriting almost his. Beat: fate as bureaucracy; violation.

chapters.title: Running
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. He tries to flee town; the road loops back past the school no matter which way he drives. His reflection now moves independently, mouthing words he cannot hear. Beat: trap closes; despair.

chapters.title: The Taken
chapters.summary: POV Ines. Through a hand mirror, Ines speaks with her brother — still aware, still waiting. He describes the Gleaner: patient, hungry, bound by the song's terms. He begs her not to come. Beat: the trapped are alive; stakes sharpen.

chapters.title: October Opens
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. Harvest festival preparations begin; the town grows warm, generous, festive — fattening the year. Students stop coming to class one by one, each leaving a drawing. Beat: horror dressed as celebration.

chapters.title: Petra Goes Quiet
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. Petra is taken during assembly while the whole town sings; only Wendell sees her hand pressed flat against the gymnasium window from outside the glass. Beat: rage crystallizes into resolve.

chapters.title: The Unlatched Door
chapters.summary: POV Ines. Ines reveals her brother's discovery: the song frees the taken only if someone inside holds the door open from within — someone must stay. They argue; both intend to be the one. Beat: love against duty at full tension.

chapters.title: Descent into Glass
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. On harvest night Wendell steps through the schoolhouse mirror, singing the first verses to hold the Gleaner's attention, and finds the taken children in a corridor of silver fog. Beat: crossing over; awe and terror.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. Inside, Wendell teaches the children the final verse while the Gleaner circles, wearing the faces of past teachers. His own voice begins harmonizing without permission. Beat: climax begins; selfhood under siege.

chapters.title: Sung Wrong, Sung Right
chapters.summary: POV alternating. The children sing; the glass shatters outward; Ines sings the anchor lines from outside, bleeding from the ears, holding the door. The Gleaner demands its owed name. Beat: climax peak — sacrifice declared.

chapters.title: The Price of Survival
chapters.summary: POV Ines. The children cross out; Wendell turns to stay, but Ines wedges the brass bell in the frame — Aldous's gift, a loophole in the terms — and the ledger burns its final page rather than break contract. Wendell falls through, changed, half-reflective. Beat: costly mercy, not free victory.

chapters.title: Twenty-Six Desks
chapters.summary: POV Wendell, epilogue. Spring term: all twenty-six students attend, the mirrors lag no more, and the town's ledgers sit unopened. Wendell still casts a faint second shadow, and each dusk he counts the doors — twenty-two now, one left deliberately unlatched. Beat: bittersweet resolution, vigilance as love.
